about: Cloud reference catalog for shaping and lighting work. One entry per photo folder. Altitudes are typical mid-latitude cloud-base heights above ground. 'size' uses the WMO hand rule: the apparent size of one cloud element held against the sky at arm's length, measured more than 30 degrees above the horizon. Personal photos live outside git in artifacts/research/cloud-photos/<id>/ (main checkout); Wikimedia Commons references are listed per entry with license and source page.

viewTags.ground: Shot from the ground looking up or out.
viewTags.ground-horizon: From the ground, cloud near the horizon, so depth and layering read.
viewTags.aerial-above: From a plane or mountain, looking down on cloud tops.
viewTags.aerial-level: From a plane at cloud height, looking across the layer.
viewTags.aerial-below: From a plane, looking up at a higher layer.
viewTags.orbit: From space or very high altitude.

timeTags.golden: Sun under about 10 degrees, warm light.
timeTags.sunset: Sun at or just under the horizon. Clouds lit from below.
timeTags.blue-hour: Sun 4 to 8 degrees below the horizon. Only high cloud still lit.

types.name: Fair-weather cumulus
types.size: Each cloud is about a fist or larger at arm's length.
types.spotIt: Small, separate cotton puffs with flat grey bottoms that all sit at the same height. Wider than they are tall. Lots of blue sky between them. Typical late-morning summer sky.

confusedWith.tell: Mediocris is about as tall as it is wide. Humilis is clearly flattened.
Stratocumulus cells touch and form a sheet. Humilis puffs are separate.

shape.silhouette: Flattened dome on a flat base.
shape.edges: Sharp, cauliflower outline on top. Clean flat base.
shape.interior: A few soft billows. Little internal shadowing.
shape.field: Evenly scattered. Bases all share one condensation level, so they line up toward the horizon.

types.light: Bright white sunlit tops, light grey bases. Thin enough that the sun side and shadow side differ only slightly. Silver lining when backlit.
types.fromAbove: White popcorn scattered over the ground, each puff casting a dark shadow on the terrain. Very common from a plane on climb-out.
types.atSunset: Turns gold then pink on the sun side. Bases go dark blue-grey quickly.

shaping.verticalProfile: Fast rise from a hard base, rounded top, peak density in the lower third.
shaping.notes: Shared flat base height across the field is the main realism cue. Base should be sharper than the top. Low density, so light diffuses through in a few hundred metres.

photoTargets: Puff field down to the horizon with bases lining up
Single puff backlit with silver edge
From a plane: shadows on the ground

types.name: Medium cumulus
types.size: Two fists or more at arm's length.
types.spotIt: Puffy clouds as tall as they are wide, with lumpy cauliflower tops and flat darker bases. Bigger and chunkier than fair-weather puffs, but no tall towers yet.

confusedWith.tell: Humilis is wider than tall.
Congestus is clearly taller than wide and towers.

shape.silhouette: Rounded heap, roughly square in profile.
shape.edges: Crisp sprouting bulges at the top. Ragged or flat at the base.
shape.interior: Several rising cells visible as separate rounded lobes with shadowed creases between them.
shape.field: Scattered to broken. Sometimes lines up in rows along the wind (cloud streets).

types.light: Strong contrast: brilliant sunlit lobes, deep grey creases and bases. Self-shadowing between lobes is obvious.
types.fromAbove: Lumpy white domes with clear shadow sides. From a plane at cloud height they look like a range of white hills.
types.atSunset: Tops lit orange while the base and lower half go dark. A strong test of light falling off with depth.

shaping.verticalProfile: Hard base, density holds through the middle, rounded top.
shaping.erosion: Billowy, with a medium-scale lobe pattern visible in silhouette.
shaping.notes: Creases between lobes need dark self-shadow but a bright powder-like rim. Good test for multiple scattering versus single scattering.

photoTargets: Side view near the horizon with shadow side
Sunset with lit tops and dark bases

types.name: Towering cumulus
types.size: Fills a large part of the view. Height is the giveaway.
types.spotIt: A tall cauliflower tower, clearly taller than it is wide, with hard sharp edges and bright sprouting tops. Often a precursor to a thunderstorm. No smooth anvil on top yet.

confusedWith.tell: Cumulonimbus has a smooth, fibrous or flat-spreading top (anvil). Congestus tops are still sharp and bubbly.
Mediocris is about as tall as wide.

shape.silhouette: Tower or stack of towers, sometimes leaning with wind shear.
shape.interior: Nested billows at many scales. Deep shadowed canyons between turrets.
shape.field: Usually a few big ones among smaller cumulus.

types.light: Extreme range: blinding white turret tops, dark undersides. Thick enough that the base can look grey-blue in full sun.
types.fromAbove: From a plane: tall white columns poking above the haze layer or a lower deck. Iconic aerial shot.
types.atSunset: Tall towers keep sunlight on their tops long after the ground is in shadow: pink and orange tops over a blue-grey base.

shaping.verticalProfile: Dense core from base to near top. Top made of separate rounded turrets.
shaping.erosion: Billowy at several scales. Worley detail should stack (large lobes carrying smaller lobes).
shaping.notes: Can lean downwind with height. Height is the main difference from mediocris, so the vertical extent of the density profile must be adjustable per cloud type.

photoTargets: From a plane: towers through haze

types.name: Thunderstorm cloud
types.size: Huge. Often fills the sky or sits on the horizon as a mountain of cloud.
types.spotIt: A giant tower whose top has gone smooth, fibrous or flat. The classic sign is the anvil: a flat sheet spreading sideways from the top. Dark, often rainy base. Can have mammatus or a shelf cloud.

confusedWith.tell: No smooth or fibrous top on congestus.
Nimbostratus is a featureless grey layer, not a tower.

shape.silhouette: Tower plus a wide flat or fibrous anvil. Anvil often overshoots downwind.
shape.edges: Lower tower is sharp cauliflower. Upper part and anvil turn fibrous and smooth (ice).
shape.interior: Huge internal shadowing. Rain shafts below the base.
shape.field: Isolated cells or a line of storms.

types.light: From far away the tower is white and the anvil is pale. Underneath it is very dark, sometimes green-grey. Lightning lights it from inside at night.
types.fromAbove: From a plane: bright towers with the anvil spreading at your altitude or above. Overshooting tops bubble up through the anvil.
types.atSunset: Anvils catch light long after sunset and glow pink or orange, with the dark tower below. Very photogenic and a hard lighting test.

shaping.verticalProfile: Dense through the full troposphere. The anvil is a wide, thinner layer at the top.
shaping.erosion: Billowy low down, fading to wispy or smooth at the anvil.
shaping.notes: Needs a shape that changes with height (billowy to fibrous) and an anvil that spreads with wind at altitude. The project's storm and lightning work (P6) targets this type.

photoTargets: Whole storm with anvil on the horizon
From a plane: anvil at eye level

types.name: Stratocumulus
types.size: Each cell is about a fist or larger at arm's length.
types.spotIt: A lumpy grey-and-white blanket of rounded clumps or rolls that mostly touch each other. Often grey on the bottom with gaps of blue. The most common cloud on Earth.

confusedWith.tell: Altocumulus cells are smaller, about a thumb wide, because they are higher.
Stratus has no lumps or cells.
Cumulus puffs are separate with clear blue between them.

shape.silhouette: Flat-topped sheet made of joined cells or rolls.
shape.edges: Soft, rounded. Tops are flat at the inversion.
shape.interior: Cellular pattern with darker thick centres and thinner bright gaps.
shape.field: Covers large areas. Rolls often line up perpendicular to the wind.

types.light: Shading varies across the cells: thick parts dark grey, thin parts bright. Sun breaks through the gaps as spots and rays.
types.fromAbove: The classic view out of the plane window: a white, gently lumpy cotton floor stretching to the horizon, sometimes with open cells. Tops are flat and brightly lit.
types.atSunset: Undersides light up orange and red when the sun is below the deck from the ground view. Great for the sunset-colour work.

shaping.verticalProfile: Thin layer with a flat top (inversion) and slightly lumpy base.
shaping.erosion: Billowy at low amplitude. Cell pattern at a 1 to 3 km scale.
shaping.notes: Flat-topped cloud deck seen from above is the main plane-flight demo backdrop. Gaps between cells must keep their structure at long distance.

photoTargets: From a plane: the cloud floor to the horizon
From the ground: rolls with blue gaps

types.name: Altocumulus
types.size: Each element is about one to three fingers wide at arm's length.
types.spotIt: A layer of many small white or light grey puffs, ripples or rows, often in a regular pattern like fish scales (mackerel sky). Higher and finer than stratocumulus, puffier and with more shading than cirrocumulus.

confusedWith.tell: Stratocumulus elements are about a fist wide.
Cirrocumulus grains are smaller than a little finger and have no shading.

shape.silhouette: Thin layer of many small elements.
shape.edges: Soft-sided puffs with slight shading on one side.
shape.interior: Regular cells, rolls or waves (undulatus). Castellanus has tiny turrets.
shape.field: Patchy to extensive. Patterns can stretch across the whole sky.

types.light: Mostly white with grey shading. Can show iridescence or a corona near the sun.
types.fromAbove: From a plane above it: a dotted or rippled layer with the ground or a lower deck visible through the gaps.
types.atSunset: One of the best sunset clouds. The whole layer can go orange, pink and purple at once.

shaping.coverage: 0.3 to 0.8, with a regular cellular mask.
shaping.erosion: Moderately billowy at a small scale.
shaping.notes: Needs a regular cellular pattern at the layer scale, not only noise. A mid layer between cumulus and cirrus. Relevant to the sunset-colour comparison with Takram.

photoTargets: From a plane: dotted layer with ground visible

types.name: Altostratus
types.spotIt: A grey or blue-grey veil over all or most of the sky. The sun looks like it is behind frosted glass: a dim disk with no halo and no shadows on the ground.

confusedWith.tell: Cirrostratus is thinner, whiter, the sun is still bright and casts shadows, and there may be a halo.
Nimbostratus is darker, lower and fully hides the sun, usually with steady rain.

shape.edges: No clear edges. Sometimes faint streaks or fibres.
shape.field: Covers the sky. Often arrives ahead of a warm front.

types.light: Flat, diffuse light. The sun disk is visible but dull.
types.fromAbove: From a plane: a flat grey-white sheet, sometimes multi-layered with lower clouds beneath.
types.atSunset: Can glow evenly yellow or orange across the underside when the sun is low.

shaping.notes: Mostly a lighting and transmittance test: how much sun gets through and how flat the sky light becomes.

types.name: Rain layer
types.spotIt: A dark grey, featureless sky with steady rain or snow. No sun visible at all. Often ragged dark scud clouds float underneath.

confusedWith.tell: Stratus is lower and lighter and gives drizzle, not steady rain.
With altostratus you can still find the sun.

shape.silhouette: Thick sheet without a clear base.
shape.interior: Featureless. Darker patches where rain is heavier.
shape.field: Covers the whole sky for hours.

types.light: Very dim, flat, grey. Blue-grey tint.
types.fromAbove: From a plane: a thick, flat, often layered white top. Inside it is grey and featureless (turbulence on climb).
types.atSunset: Little colour. Sometimes a strip of orange at a clear gap on the horizon.

shaping.verticalProfile: Thick and uniform with a soft base.
shaping.notes: Mainly a fog, precipitation and ambient-light test. Low priority for shaping.

photoTargets: Horizon gap at sunset under the deck

types.name: Stratus, fog and valley fog
types.spotIt: A low, flat grey layer like fog that does not touch the ground, or real fog sitting in valleys. From a hilltop or plane you see a white sea of cloud filling the valleys with hills sticking out.

confusedWith.tell: Stratocumulus has lumps and cells.
Nimbostratus is thicker and darker with steady rain.

shape.silhouette: Flat sheet that follows the terrain. In valleys it pools like a liquid.
shape.edges: Diffuse, feathered where it meets ridges.
shape.field: Fills low ground. Edges wrap around hills.

types.light: From below: flat white-grey. From above: brilliant white with soft blue shadows from the terrain.
types.fromAbove: Valley fog or a cloud sea seen from a mountain or plane. Hills poke through as islands. Very relevant to the onsen valley demo.
types.atSunset: Fog tops turn pink and gold. Sunrise valley fog is a classic shot.

shaping.verticalProfile: Thin, flat top, density tied to height above terrain.
shaping.erosion: Wispy and soft. Very low billowiness.
shaping.notes: Needs a height-above-ground density term, not only an altitude band. Edge fade against ridges is the realism cue.

photoTargets: Sunrise fog with peaks as islands
Low stratus over a city or coast

types.name: Cirrus
types.size: Thin strands across large parts of the sky.
types.spotIt: Thin white wispy strands or hooks like brush strokes or horse tails, high in a blue sky. Made of ice, so they look silky with no shading.

confusedWith.tell: Cirrostratus is a smooth sheet. Cirrus is separate strands.
Cirrocumulus is tiny grains, not strands.

shape.silhouette: Streaks, hooks (uncinus) and fallstreaks curving with wind shear.
shape.interior: Parallel fibres. Denser heads with trailing tails.
shape.field: Patches or bands, often all aligned in one direction.

types.light: White in daylight with no shadow side. Often catches colour first and last around sunrise and sunset.
types.fromAbove: Usually above the plane. From cruise altitude it can be at eye level as faint haze bands.
types.atSunset: Among the first to light up and the last to fade. Strands go gold, then red, then pink against a darkening sky.

shaping.verticalProfile: Very thin layer or a 2D sky-shell layer.
shaping.erosion: Wispy (curl or flow noise stretched along wind).
shaping.notes: Usually rendered as a 2D high layer with anisotropic, wind-stretched noise. The hooks come from shear. Main contributor to sunset colour after the sun is down.

types.name: Cirrocumulus
types.size: Each grain is smaller than a little finger's width at arm's length.
types.spotIt: Tiny white grains or ripples in rows, like sand ripples on a beach, very high up. No grey shading at all.

confusedWith.tell: Altocumulus elements are larger (one to three fingers) and have shading.
Cirrus is strands, not grains.

shape.silhouette: Thin patch of tiny regular grains or ripples.
shape.field: Usually patches, often with cirrus nearby.

types.light: Pure white, no shading. Can show iridescence near the sun.
types.atSunset: Fine pink texture across the sky.

shaping.erosion: Small-scale regular cellular or ripple pattern.
shaping.notes: A 2D high-layer pattern. Test for fine texture at a distance without aliasing.

types.name: Cirrostratus
types.spotIt: A thin milky veil over the sky. The sun is still bright and things still cast shadows. Often makes a ring (22-degree halo) around the sun or moon.

confusedWith.tell: Altostratus is thicker and greyer, the sun is dull and there is no halo.
Cirrus is separate strands.

shape.edges: Hard to see. Fades out gradually.
shape.field: Whole sky. Often arrives before a warm front.

types.light: Whitens the blue sky. Halos and sun dogs.
types.fromAbove: Usually above the plane, as a milky sky.
types.atSunset: Washes the whole sky in soft colour.

shaping.notes: Sky-tint and transmittance only. Halos would need an ice-crystal phase function, out of scope for now.

photoTargets: Milky sky with sharp shadows on the ground

types.name: Lenticular cloud
types.size: Varies. Smooth lens or UFO shape.
types.spotIt: A smooth lens, saucer or stack of plates, usually near or downwind of mountains. Stays in one place while the wind blows through it.

confusedWith.tell: Ordinary altocumulus is lumpy and in many elements.

shape.silhouette: Smooth lens, often stacked like plates.
shape.field: Single or a few, tied to terrain.

types.light: Smooth gradients, bright rims, iridescence sometimes.
types.fromAbove: From a plane: smooth lenses at or above flight level near mountains.
types.atSunset: Smooth surfaces take colour evenly. Very dramatic.

shaping.notes: Good candidate for an artist-authored VDB hero cloud, because procedural noise fields struggle with smooth stacked lenses.

types.name: Mammatus
types.size: Each pouch is roughly a fist wide.
types.spotIt: Rounded pouches hanging down from the underside of a cloud, usually under a thunderstorm anvil. Most dramatic around sunset when they glow orange.

confusedWith.tell: Stratocumulus lumps bulge up and sideways. Mammatus pouches hang down.

shape.interior: Smooth pouches with strong shading between them.
shape.field: Underside of an anvil or a thick layer.

types.light: Lit from the side or below at sunset. The shading between pouches is the whole look.
types.atSunset: Iconic orange glow on the pouches.

shaping.verticalProfile: Inverted billows on the base of a layer.
shaping.notes: Needs a base shape that bulges downward, the opposite of normal cumulus. Optional stretch goal for storms.

photoTargets: Under an anvil after a storm

types.name: Shelf cloud
types.spotIt: A long low wedge or shelf on the leading edge of a storm, dark underneath with layered tiers. Looks like a wall or a wave rolling toward you. Gusty winds arrive right under it.

confusedWith.tell: The shelf is a low feature at the front of a cumulonimbus, not the whole storm.

shape.silhouette: Low horizontal wedge with stepped tiers.
shape.field: A line along the storm front.

types.light: Dark underside with a bright gap of clear sky beneath it.

shaping.notes: Storm-front drama. Stretch goal. Would likely need an authored shape.

types.name: From the plane window
types.latin: View category, any low or middle cloud
types.size: Seen from above or at the same level.
types.spotIt: Any photo out of a plane window or from a high mountain where you look down on or across cloud tops. Sort by what you see: a flat cotton floor is usually stratocumulus or stratus; separate white puffs are cumulus; tall columns are congestus or cumulonimbus. Put the photo here and tag the type too.

shape.silhouette: Depends on the cloud type underneath.
shape.edges: Tops are sunlit and crisp in cumulus, soft in stratus.
shape.interior: Shadows cast by taller clouds onto lower ones and onto the ground.
shape.field: Aerial perspective: contrast and colour fade to blue haze with distance. Earth curvature at the horizon at cruise altitude.

types.light: Direct sun on tops, so very bright. Haze grows with distance. Glory (a rainbow ring around the plane's shadow) sometimes visible.
types.atSunset: The deck turns gold and pink, with a bright horizon band and a dark blue sky above.

shaping.verticalProfile: Look for flat tops (inversion), turrets poking through and multiple layers.
shaping.notes: Primary reference for the plains plane-flight demo. Key cues: distance haze on clouds, cloud shadows on lower layers and ground, tops that stay crisp at long range, and the horizon line.

photoTargets: Flying through a gap between layers

types.name: Sunset and sunrise colour
types.spotIt: Any sky with sunset or sunrise colour on the clouds. The best ones show several layers at different heights in different colours: high cirrus still pink while lower clouds are already grey.

shape.edges: Edges facing the sun glow first.
shape.interior: Underside lighting when the sun is below the cloud base.
shape.field: Layering by height is the point: each layer loses the sun at a different time.

types.light: The sun's light passes through a long path of atmosphere, so it reaches the clouds already orange or red. Higher clouds stay lit longer. Shadowed parts pick up blue and violet from the sky.
types.fromAbove: From a plane, the deck below turns warm while the sky above goes deep blue.

shaping.notes: Highest priority for lighting: this is where Takram currently beats us. Compare layer-by-height colour, underlit bases, and the blue ambient fill in shadows. Record the time relative to sunset if you know it.

photoTargets: Multiple layers at different heights with different colours

types.name: Sun rays and silver linings
types.spotIt: Beams of light and shadow fanning out from behind a cloud, or a bright glowing edge around a cloud that sits in front of the sun.

shape.silhouette: Rays radiate from the sun's position.
shape.edges: The silver lining is a thin bright rim where light scatters forward through the thin edge.
shape.interior: Dark centre of the cloud against a bright rim.
shape.field: Needs haze or dust in the air for rays to show.

types.light: Strong forward scattering at cloud edges, plus light shafts in hazy air.
types.fromAbove: Shafts falling through gaps in a deck.
types.atSunset: Rays are most visible near sunset.

shaping.notes: Tests the phase function (forward lobe), thin-edge transmittance and volumetric shadows in the atmosphere (god rays).

photoTargets: Backlit cloud with a bright rim
